title: A closed-loop control that sets axial eye growth

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to regulate the eye’s front-to-back growth throughout childhood and adolescence so that its developing size remains appropriate for clear distance vision without refractive correction. The biological starting point is emmetropization: a feedback process in which retinal image defocus supplies information that helps guide postnatal refractive development. The intended advance is durable control of that process, with an identifiable mechanism and no excessive catch-up growth after treatment ends.

Here, setting axial growth means maintaining an appropriate developmental trajectory, rather than freezing the eye at one length. Normal eyes also elongate during childhood, and axial length alone does not determine whether an eye is emmetropic. A treatment would therefore need to coordinate growth with refractive development. An optical intervention, a drug, or another biological approach could supply the capability; the defining feature is the durable regulation achieved.

Conceptual distinction: sustained growth within an emmetropic range would demonstrate a valuable clinical outcome, but would not by itself prove a selectable axial set point or restored closed-loop feedback. The stronger interpretation of this innovation requires evidence that growth changes appropriately when the eye deviates from its target and settles back toward that target. These remain proposed capabilities, not achievements established by the supplied evidence.

significance.text: Durable control could shift myopia care toward preventing excessive elongation during development. The immediate consequence would be less excess axial growth, with the potential to reduce progression toward high myopia. Earlier onset is associated with greater myopia in adulthood, making childhood intervention consequential. Conventional single-vision spectacles correct blur; specialized myopia-control spectacles can also slow elongation. The proposed advance would extend beyond those demonstrated partial effects by sustaining appropriate development through adolescence and after withdrawal.

The original research motivates population-scale prevention using a 2016 projection attributed to Holden and colleagues: 4,758 million people with myopia in 2050, equivalent to 49.8% of the world population, including 938 million with high myopia. These are future projections, not observed prevalence. Their numerical accuracy cannot be verified from the supplied source copy, which contains only redirect text. The figures remain an explicitly unverified part of the original rationale rather than an established quantitative basis for this record.

Conditional impact synthesis: preventing excessive elongation could reduce later vision-threatening disease, but a growth-control trial would not itself establish prevention of permanent blindness. The original research names retinal detachment, myopic maculopathy, and glaucoma as relevant complications; its retained Holden source does not substantiate those individual associations here. The size of any reduction in those outcomes would require long-term clinical evidence. A safe and practical intervention could have population-scale value, but guaranteed elimination of myopia-related blindness is not supported.

Scope distinction: a drug that maintained appropriate developmental growth could qualify, whereas complete arrest of normal axial growth would not automatically do so. Preventing further elongation would also not demonstrate reversal of an established staphyloma, a localized pathological deformation of the eye wall. Restoring that anatomy is a separate proposed repair problem; the supplied material does not establish the additional biomechanical intervention it would require.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability is reliable, durable control of developmental eye growth toward an emmetropic trajectory, with a mechanism that explains how treatment regulates growth and why the benefit persists. Existing interventions already modify axial elongation, so the barrier is not absolute biological uncontrollability. It is the gap between partial modification and dependable regulation over the full period of growth.

A central scientific barrier is understanding how retinal detection of defocus is translated into growth inhibition and changes in the tissues governing eye size. The 2024 review summarizes reduced inhibitory responses to positive defocus in myopic eyes, but the reported short-term experiments do not establish that the inhibitory pathway is completely or permanently lost. The 2025 IMI review likewise identifies unresolved mechanisms; even a direct scleral action of atropine remains debated. A controllable pathway must therefore be identified without assuming that one universal defect explains all myopia.

Engineering synthesis: a practical controller would need a measurable developmental target, a way to detect meaningful deviations, and an intervention whose effect can be adjusted without suppressing normal growth or compromising vision. It would also need to distinguish sustained regulation from temporary suppression followed by rebound. Demonstrating a selectable target would require showing that different justified targets produce predictable responses, rather than inferring control from one favorable average treatment effect.

Long treatment duration, safety during development, and behavior after cessation are concrete translational barriers. These are especially relevant because an intervention can slow elongation while still having an unacceptable safety profile or substantial rebound. The supplied IMI review reports both safety concerns and significant rebound after cessation for red-light therapy, illustrating why efficacy during treatment alone is insufficient.

current_state.text: Schaeffel and Swiatczak’s July 2024 Vision Research review summarizes short-term human experiments indicating that emmetropic eyes respond differently to the two signs of defocus and that myopic eyes show reduced growth inhibition under positive defocus, when the image plane lies in front of the retina. The authors interpret these findings as impaired inhibitory feedback and describe myopia development in open-loop terms. That interpretation should not be generalized into proof that all myopic eyes permanently lose feedback regulation.

The available support for those findings is the identified institutional publication page containing the abstract. The supplied Vision Research DOI artifact contains only redirect text, and the publisher’s full scientific content was not independently available in the supplied review. The abstract supports the narrower experimental findings, but does not provide the basis for a comprehensive assessment of methods, effect sizes, or long-term responses.

The September 2025 International Myopia Institute review by Bullimore and colleagues covers publications through the end of 2024. It documents slowing of axial elongation with overnight orthokeratology, soft contact lenses including dual-focus designs, specialized spectacle lenslets, atropine, and red-light therapy. For orthokeratology, it reports median one-year efficacy of 0.17 mm, with an interquartile range of 0.13–0.20 mm, and median two-year efficacy of 0.30 mm. These values represent reduced elongation relative to comparison groups over the stated intervals, not absolute growth targets or interchangeable annual rates.

The same review reports that highly aspherical lenslet spectacles reduced myopia progression by 0.80 diopters and axial elongation by 0.35 mm relative to single-vision spectacles in the cited comparison. The supplied review excerpt does not specify that comparison’s duration, so these values should not be annualized. Effects differ by intervention and follow-up period. Red-light therapy is described as substantially slowing progression, with material qualifications concerning safety and significant rebound after cessation.

These dated findings establish partial clinical control and continuing mechanistic questions. They do not establish durable, selectable set-point control, but neither do they prove that no qualifying intervention existed by November 1, 2026. The supplied material contains no freshness search record, and the retained IMI text is truncated during its surgical section. Its available treatment discussions remain useful evidence, while its coverage and extraction limits prevent an exhaustive claim about the contemporary frontier.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: a randomized trial would enroll children at risk of excessive axial elongation and test a defined intervention through adolescence. It would prespecify age-appropriate emmetropic growth ranges, assess both axial length and refractive development, and show that treatment maintains appropriate development safely over that interval. Comparison with age-matched emmetropic growth is grounded in the IMI review’s discussion of efficacy measurement; the full trial requirement proposed here is not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized trial maintains safe emmetropic development through adolescence

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability demonstration: withdrawal follow-up would have a prespecified duration long enough to assess clinically meaningful catch-up growth, using a defined comparator and an explicit boundary for excess growth. A one- or two-year reduction resembling existing partial-treatment effects would not satisfy this innovation’s proposed through-adolescence criterion. The supplied evidence does not determine the necessary withdrawal interval or numerical rebound boundary; those would need justification before the trial.
completion_criteria.label: Withdrawal follow-up demonstrates catch-up growth stays within justified excess-growth boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanistic demonstration: an identifiable causal pathway would connect the intervention to regulated growth. To substantiate the closed-loop and set-point claims, investigators would additionally show appropriate corrective responses to safely assessed deviations from the target, with evidence that regulation weakens as the error resolves. Maintaining an average growth rate alone would establish neither feedback restoration nor target selectability.
completion_criteria.label: Causal feedback corrects deviations and weakens as errors resolve

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent studies would reproduce the effect across prespecified ages, baseline refractive states, and participant groups, while documenting adverse effects, treatment burden, adherence, and situations in which control fails. Finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth within those populations and conditions, not universal effectiveness. Prevention of late retinal disease or blindness would require additional long-term outcome evidence, and reversal of existing pathological deformation would remain outside the demonstrated capability unless tested separately.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication establishes population breadth and documents practical control limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OPH-02, Biological reconstruction of foveal cones, RPE, and their blood supply, and OPH-08, Reperfusion of established retinal capillary dropout, address retinal tissue or vascular repair. OPH-06 instead concerns regulation of developmental eye size. Their shared interest in preserving retinal function does not make growth control a substitute for reconstructing damaged tissue or restoring lost perfusion.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-01, Retinotopic reconnection of retinal ganglion cell axons to brain targets, OPH-05, Patterned vision from the brain when the eye cannot send signals, and OPH-10, Arrest of glaucomatous ganglion-cell death when pressure is not the lever, concern neural connectivity, visual substitution, or neuronal survival. Retinal signaling is relevant to OPH-06’s feedback mechanism, but regulating elongation would not demonstrate axon reconnection, brain-generated patterned vision, or pressure-independent protection against glaucoma.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-03, Reversal of established cataract without removing the lens, and OPH-04, A manufactured cornea that clears vascularized stromal opacity, address optical clarity in different structures. OPH-06 addresses the developmental relationship between eye size and refractive state. Restoring transparency would not by itself establish controlled axial growth, and controlling growth would not remove lens or corneal opacity.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-07, One programmable repair for many photoreceptor and RPE gene defects, concerns a broadly adaptable repair platform. A genetic intervention could hypothetically contribute to OPH-06 if it achieved durable growth regulation, but repairing multiple inherited retinal defects is a separate scope. OPH-09, Reopening of the human visual critical period, shares an interest in developmental plasticity while targeting visual-system learning rather than eye size; evidence for either capability would not establish the other.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-11, Prevention of progression from early or intermediate AMD to late AMD, shares OPH-06’s preventive aim but concerns a different disease process and stage of life. Neither concept’s success would establish the other. Within OPH-06, existing optical and pharmacological myopia treatments are possible routes toward the proposed capability if they eventually meet its durability and feedback criteria; they are not additional roster entries to merge or remove.

change_log.reason: Normal emmetropic eyes elongate during childhood, and axial length alone does not determine refractive state.

change_log.change: Replaced universal inhibitory-feedback failure with reduced responses documented in short-term experiments.
change_log.reason: The institutional abstract supports impaired inhibition and an open-loop interpretation, not permanent or complete failure in all myopia.

change_log.change: Separated durable clinical regulation from proof of a selectable set point or restored closed-loop control.
change_log.reason: Matching an emmetropic growth trajectory does not alone demonstrate corrective responses to target deviations.

change_log.change: Replaced absolute molecular uncontrollability with unresolved mechanisms and a gap between partial treatment and durable regulation.
change_log.reason: Existing optical and pharmacological interventions already modify axial growth.

change_log.reason: Cumulative treatment effects cannot be treated as constant annual rates.

change_log.reason: The blanket claim that spectacles only correct blur overlooks demonstrated slowing with specialized designs.

change_log.reason: Reduced elongation does not itself establish prevention of late clinical complications or repair of established deformation.

change_log.change: Added explicit proposed criteria for developmental safety, withdrawal follow-up, mechanism, reproducibility, and demonstrated scope.
change_log.reason: These make the intended capability assessable without presenting proposed thresholds as accepted standards.

change_log.change: Preserved source-access limits and removed categorical claims about the November 2026 frontier.
change_log.reason: The institutional source is abstract-only, the DOI artifacts are redirect-only, the IMI extraction is truncated, and no freshness search record was supplied.

unresolved_issues: Whether any intervention met the proposed durable-control criteria by November 1, 2026 remains unassessed; the supplied IMI review covers publications only through the end of 2024.
The molecular pathway linking defocus detection to sustained growth regulation, including the relevant scleral effects, remains incompletely established in the supplied evidence.
Whether short-term reduced inhibitory responses explain long-term progression across different forms of myopia remains unresolved.
The age-specific target ranges, trial duration, withdrawal follow-up interval, and acceptable rebound boundary require prospective justification.
The duration associated with the reported lenslet effects of 0.80 diopters and 0.35 mm is not specified in the supplied review excerpt.

The reviewer’s recommendation to remove the Holden projections was not adopted literally: they were retained as explicitly unverified attributed projections to preserve useful original quantitative detail. Their accuracy and the original complication assertions remain unverified by the redirect-only artifact.
The magnitude of any eventual reduction in retinal complications or permanent blindness would require long-term clinical evidence.
The requirements for reversing an established staphyloma are not established by the supplied sources and remain separate from growth regulation.

brief.title: Lasting control of eye growth for clear distance vision
possible: Children could grow up with eyes that keep developing toward clear distance vision without corrective lenses. Treatment would guide the eye’s front-to-back growth through adolescence, with benefits that persist after treatment stops.
The eye would respond when growth strays from an appropriate target, then ease that response as it returns toward the target. Normal childhood growth would continue.
why: For children at risk of myopia, or nearsightedness, lasting growth control could prevent excessive eye lengthening and reduce progression toward severe myopia. Starting early matters because earlier onset is associated with worse nearsightedness in adulthood.

sources.showed: This work projects the future worldwide prevalence of nearsightedness and severe nearsightedness.
sources.cited_for: It supports the population-scale rationale for prevention.
sources.not_established: A population projection does not demonstrate control of eye growth.

sources.showed: Their review describes short-term human experiments in which nearsighted eyes responded less strongly to blur that normally inhibits growth.
sources.quote: (2) Strikingly, the myopic retina has reduced ability to inhibit eye growth when positive defocus is imposed.
sources.cited_for: It supports the idea that weakened responses to blur may contribute to excessive eye growth.
sources.not_established: Short-term responses do not establish permanent loss of growth regulation or a way to restore it.

sources.showed: Their review finds that several treatments slow nearsightedness and eye lengthening, including specialized lenses and atropine, a drug used in eye drops.
sources.quote: The overall conclusion is that there are multiple effective interventions in most categories.
sources.cited_for: It establishes that treatments can already slow excessive eye growth.
sources.not_established: Slower growth during treatment does not establish lasting regulation toward a chosen target after treatment ends.

shown: The International Myopia Institute review by Bullimore and colleagues documents partial control: specialized glasses, contact lenses and drug treatments can slow eye lengthening. It also reports safety concerns and substantial catch-up growth after red-light treatment stops.

Schaeffel and Swiatczak describe short-term experiments showing that nearsighted eyes respond less strongly to growth-inhibiting blur. This identifies a possible weakness in the eye’s natural growth regulation.
missing: A treatment has yet to demonstrate safe, appropriate eye growth and focusing development throughout adolescence.
Lasting benefit after treatment ends has yet to be demonstrated without excessive catch-up growth.
A known biological pathway must connect treatment to growth that corrects deviations from selectable, justified targets.
Independent studies must establish who benefits, the treatment burden and the conditions in which control fails.

milestones.label: Safe eye development through adolescence
milestones.explanation: A trial assigning children to groups by chance would have to show safe growth and focusing development within age-appropriate ranges through adolescence. This would establish sustained clinical benefit.

milestones.label: Lasting benefit after treatment stops
milestones.explanation: Follow-up after withdrawal would have to show catch-up growth stays within justified limits against a defined comparison. This would distinguish lasting benefit from temporary slowing.

milestones.label: Growth corrects deviations from chosen targets
milestones.explanation: A known biological pathway would have to correct deviations from chosen targets, with responses weakening as the gap closes. This would establish feedback control, where the response depends on the remaining error.

milestones.label: Independent confirmation across groups and practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to reproduce control across defined ages, starting vision states and participant groups, while documenting harms, burden and failures. This would establish its demonstrated reach and limits.

uncertain: Does the weaker short-term response to growth-inhibiting blur explain long-term progression across different forms of nearsightedness?
Which growth targets, follow-up periods and limits on catch-up growth would justify calling the control durable?
How much would lasting growth control reduce later vision-threatening disease?

page.title: Closed-loop regulation of axial eye growth
page.definition: An intervention maintains emmetropization, the feedback process that matches the eye’s front-to-back length to its focusing power, through adolescence and after treatment withdrawal. Retinal defocus drives corrective growth that diminishes as the focusing error resolves.

goal.need: In 2000 an estimated 163 million people worldwide had high myopia, which raises the risk of retinal detachment, myopic macular degeneration, glaucoma and cataract. Ordinary glasses correct blurred distance vision. Myopia-control lenses can slow elongation, but after withdrawal the eye can resume growth typical of untreated myopia. Children who kept distant images in focus as their eyes grew could avoid early myopia and its associated risk of high myopia. Whether childhood treatment prevents later sight loss remains uncertain.

figures.caption: Estimated global burden in 2000
figures.note: High myopia is a subset of myopia. These are retrospective estimates, not observed global counts.

completion.title: A pediatric intervention maintains defocus-driven growth control through adolescence and after withdrawal.
completion.criterion: In children at risk of myopia, an intervention maintains age-appropriate emmetropic refraction and axial elongation through adolescence. Positive and negative retinal defocus cause compensatory growth responses that diminish as the focusing error resolves. These responses and refractive development persist for at least 1 year after withdrawal. Cycloplegic refraction, measured with accommodation blocked, and axial biometry must support the result. Age-specific target ranges and acceptance margins require prospective justification; the cited sources do not fix them.
completion.basis: IMI reports from 2019 and 2025, the 2024 National Academies recommendations, and FDA MiSight approval and post-approval documents were searched for criteria for restored feedback, selectable axial set points and persistence through adolescence. No integrated pass/fail test was found. This provisional test combines lens compensation, the emmetropic-growth comparator and IMI’s minimum 1-year withdrawal interval; that interval alone does not validate developmental durability.

milestones.title: Developing animal eyes compensate for both positive and negative lens-imposed defocus.
milestones.criterion: In developing animal eyes, positive lenses focus images in front of the retina and slow axial elongation. Negative lenses focus images behind the retina and accelerate axial elongation. For each sign, the resulting refractive shift must reduce the error imposed by the lens. Lens power and exposure duration depend on the species.
milestones.set_by: Experimental emmetropization community, as described in sections 3.4 and 8 of the 2019 IMI experimental-models report
milestones.threshold_quote: Imposing hyperopic or myopic defocus in animal models results in compensatory changes in eye growth that reduces the imposed refractive error.

milestones.title: Human eyes shorten with +3 D defocus and lengthen with −3 D defocus after 60 minutes.
milestones.criterion: Measure optical axial length from the anterior cornea to the retinal pigment epithelium at baseline and after 60 minutes of monocular defocus. Test +3 D and −3 D on separate days, with the fellow eye optimally corrected and a separate no-defocus control condition. Mean optical axial length must decrease from baseline with +3 D and increase with −3 D. This assay measures an acute biometric response.
milestones.set_by: Human emmetropization researchers’ lens-defocus assay, recognized in IMI’s 2019 report; the 60-minute, ±3 D implementation is Read and colleagues’ published experiment
milestones.threshold_quote: Significant changes in optical axial length occurred in human subjects after 60 minutes of monocular defocus.

milestones.title: A randomized pediatric trial shows less axial elongation and myopic progression over 3 years.
milestones.criterion: Randomize children who already have myopia to treatment or a concurrent control. Compare change from baseline to three years in both primary outcomes. The treatment group must show less axial elongation and a smaller shift toward myopia in cycloplegic spherical-equivalent refraction.
milestones.set_by: CooperVision’s MiSight trial, NCT01729208, co-primary endpoints as published in 2019; IMI recommends a minimum 3-year efficacy study
milestones.threshold_quote: Primary outcome measures were the change in cycloplegic spherical equivalent refraction and axial length.

milestones.title: FDA authorizes a device for slowing myopia progression in children.
milestones.criterion: FDA authorizes marketing of the device with an indication explicitly covering slower myopia progression in children. Apply the age at treatment initiation, refractive range and other eligibility conditions in that device’s authorized labeling. An indication limited to optical correction is insufficient.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, pediatric indications for use in PMA P180035 and De Novo classification DEN250016
milestones.threshold_quote: for slowing the progression of myopia in children

milestones.title: Treatment gains persist without excess axial elongation or myopic progression for 1 year after withdrawal.
milestones.criterion: Follow children for at least one year after stopping treatment. Compare axial elongation and progression of cycloplegic spherical-equivalent refraction with rates expected in age-matched untreated myopic eyes over the same interval. Both comparisons must support retention of the accrued gain without excess progression. Report uncertainty in each difference so readers can judge how much rebound is compatible with the data.
milestones.set_by: IMI’s 2019 clinical-trial recommendations specify ≥1 year of withdrawal follow-up; its 2025 intervention report defines rebound relative to matched untreated myopic eyes
milestones.threshold_quote: Studies designed to evaluate potential rebound should have a minimum 1 year follow-up after stopping treatment

milestones.title: Fewer initially nonmyopic children develop myopia over two years with treatment than with placebo.
milestones.criterion: Compare two-year cumulative myopia incidence between randomized treatment and placebo groups. In the LAMP2 population, children are aged 4–9 years at enrollment and have baseline cycloplegic spherical-equivalent refraction from 0.00 to +1.00 D. Count onset when either eye reaches −0.50 D or more myopic under cycloplegia. The treatment group must have significantly lower cumulative incidence.
milestones.set_by: LAMP2 randomized clinical trial, ChiCTR-IPR-15006883, cumulative-incidence primary outcome
milestones.threshold_quote: Cumulative myopia incidence (defined as spherical equivalent ≤−0.50 D)

not_found: No externally specified age-specific emmetropic growth bands or statistical acceptance margins for restored feedback were located.
No pediatric study demonstrating the integrated completion criterion was located.
No National Academies or IMI statement disputing the feasibility or value of restoring durable emmetropization was located.

results.finding: MiSight trial: 109 children completed 3 years; axial elongation was 0.32 mm less with treatment than control.
results.detail: Cycloplegic spherical-equivalent change was −0.51 versus −1.24 D; both outcomes favored treatment (P < .001). One treatment participant was excluded from the 36-month analysis. Treatment withdrawal was not assessed.
results.quote:
Mean change in axial length was 0.32 mm (52%) less in the test
group than in the control group (0.30 ± 0.27 vs. 0.62 ± 0.30 mm,P < .001).

results.finding: In 10 developing chicks, the mean refractive change differed by 3.6 D between positive- and negative-lens groups.
results.detail: Axial length was measured at dissection. The untreated comparison reported interocular variation in posterior nodal distance, leaving the normal axial elongation rate unmeasured.
results.quote:
In fact, the mean
change in the measured refractive state was
3.6D.

results.finding: In 28 young adults, mean optical axial length shortened by 13 μm after 60 minutes of +3 D monocular defocus.
results.quote: A significant increase in optical axial length (mean change, +8 ± 14 μm; P = 0.03) occurred after hyperopic defocus, and a significant reduction in optical axial length (mean change, -13 ± 14 μm; P = 0.0001) was found after myopic defocus.

results.finding: In 16 adults, mean optical axial length decreased by 8 μm after one hour of positive defocus.
results.detail: All six sessions imposed continuous or alternating defocus. Each session’s baseline followed a period of clear viewing.
results.quote: The axial length then continued to shorten gradually over the next 45 minutes, reaching a significant maximum axial length reduction of -8 ± 10 μm at the end of the 60 minutes (p = 0.046)

results.finding: In 256 randomized myopic children, DOT 0.2 spectacles reduced three-year axial elongation by 0.13 mm versus single-vision controls.
results.detail: Of the 200 children who completed the 36-month visit, 71 wore DOT 0.2 and 83 wore control lenses. The DOT 0.4 arm did not show a significant benefit on either co-primary outcome.
results.quote: Test 1 spectacle lenses demonstrated superiority to the Control in both co-primary endpoints: with a difference between means (Test 1−Control) of −0.13 mm for AL (p=0.018) and 0.33 D for cSER (p=0.008) in Part 1

results.finding: In 144 randomized myopic children, MiSight reduced three-year axial elongation by 0.28 mm versus Proclear and also slowed cycloplegic refractive progression.
results.detail: The effectiveness analysis used available data from the dispensed cohort. Of 109 children who completed the study, one MiSight participant was excluded from the 36-month effectiveness analysis after starting growth hormone therapy.
results.quote:
The MiSight arm had a lower increase in mean axial length than the control by 0.28 
mm (95% CI: 0.20 to 0.36 mm).

results.finding: FDA approved MiSight 1 Day to slow myopia progression in children on November 15, 2019.
results.detail: Sample size does not apply to the approval decision.
results.quote: CDRH issued an approval order on November 15, 2019.

results.finding: Among 159 randomized children with myopia, Essilor Stellest reduced axial elongation by 0.24 mm versus single-vision lenses at two years.
results.quote:
For axial length, the test group showed a 53% 
reduction in axial elongation at 24 months, with a model-calculated difference of -0.24 mm (95% 
CI: -0.29 to -0.19 mm) compared to controls.

results.finding: FDA authorized one device, Essilor Stellest, to slow myopia progression in eligible children.

results.finding: Children who stopped MiSight (n=18) had 0.22 mm mean axial elongation over one year.
results.detail: The withdrawal group averaged 0.01 mm more elongation and 0.09 D less myopic shift than spectacle controls. The nonsignificant differences leave the magnitude of possible rebound unresolved.
results.quote: Axial length and myopia progression in the last year were 0.15± 0.11 mm, 0.22± 0.11 mm, 0.21± 0.10 mm and -0.37±0.44D, -0.46±0.39D and -0.55±0.45D for the three groups, respectively.

results.finding: Among 78 participants analyzed after MiSight withdrawal, the younger subgroup had 0.03 mm more axial elongation than predicted over one year.
results.detail: The untreated rates were extrapolated from the original control cohort. Some final visits fell outside the scheduled window, and the study annualized the measurements.
results.quote: The average 0.03 mm (standard deviation, 0.01 mm) faster than predicted measured axial growth in the younger subgroup reached significance with the Welch test (p = 0.03).

results.finding: In BLINK (294 children with myopia randomized), high-add lenses reduced three-year axial elongation by 0.23 mm versus single-vision lenses.
results.detail: The analysis plan classified secondary endpoint findings as exploratory because of multiple comparisons.
results.quote: Adjusted mean eye growth was 0.42 mm for high add power, 0.58 mm for medium add power, and 0.66 mm for single vision.

results.finding: Among 570 Chinese children with myopia who completed follow-up, axial elongation over three years was 0.89 mm less with 1% atropine than with placebo.
results.detail: The changes are calculated from Table 3. The reported analysis excluded 68 atropine and 22 placebo participants who did not complete the trial.

results.finding: Among 570 Chinese children with myopia who completed follow-up, axial elongation in the year after atropine withdrawal was 0.21 mm less than with placebo.
results.detail: Differential attrition limits the comparison. The withdrawal-year analysis included 262 of 330 children assigned to atropine and 308 of 330 assigned to placebo.

results.finding: In 60 myopic children, continuing versus stopping 0.01% atropine yielded an adjusted one-year cycloplegic refraction difference of +0.019 D.
results.detail: Children assigned to vehicle in the first three years all switched to active treatment in year 4, leaving no continuously untreated group.

results.finding: In children with myopia (144 randomized), MiSight reduced three-year axial elongation by 0.32 mm versus Proclear 1-day.
results.detail: Of 109 children who completed the trial, 108 were included in the 36-month analysis (52 MiSight, 56 control).
results.quote:
Mean change in axial length was 0.32 mm (52%) less in the test
group than in the control group (0.30 ± 0.27 vs. 0.62 ± 0.30 mm,P < .001).

results.finding: Among 78 myopic adolescents analyzed after MiSight withdrawal, the younger subgroup’s one-year axial elongation exceeded the untreated prediction by 0.03 mm.
results.detail: The younger subgroup comprised 46 eyes aged 14–16 at withdrawal. The untreated model extrapolated from the original control cohort using annual slowing of 15% for axial elongation and 10% for refractive progression.
results.quote:
The average 0.03 mm (standard deviation, 0.01 mm) 
faster than predicted measured axial growth in the younger sub -
group reached significance with the Welch test (p = 0.03).

results.finding: In 26 young adults, mean optical axial length fell 8 μm with +3 D and rose with −3 D at the 60-minute endpoint.
results.detail: The Results section gives the exact 60-minute change for +3 D and reports significant elongation at all sampled times for −3 D. Its numerical value for peak elongation is from 50 minutes.
results.quote: the baseline axial length until the end of the myopic defocus period (mean difference of −8 ± 10 μm, p = 0.037)

results.finding: In LAMP2 (474 initially nonmyopic children randomized), nightly 0.05% atropine lowered two-year cumulative myopia incidence by 24.6 percentage points versus placebo.
results.detail: The reported two-year incidence estimates use the 353 children who completed follow-up. The trial had 121 dropouts (25.5%).
results.quote: Compared with the placebo group, the 0.05% atropine group had significantly lower 2-year cumulative myopia incidence (difference, 24.6% [95% CI, 12.0%-36.4%])

results.finding: Among 235 BLINK2 completers, axial elongation was 0.08 mm/y in the year after multifocal lens withdrawal.
results.detail: The untreated benchmarks came from growth curves. A separate extrapolation from the original single-vision group estimated untreated axial elongation at 0.06 mm/y.
results.quote: The growth rate after discontinuing multifocal lenses was 0.08 mm/y and −0.22 D/y (median age, 17 years).

results.finding: Among 51 Japanese schoolchildren assessed one year after stopping 0.01% atropine or placebo, the atropine-minus-placebo difference in spherical-equivalent change was −0.13 D.
results.detail: Only 51 of 167 participants had one-year measurements. The refractive point estimate favors placebo, and neither comparison establishes equivalence.

goal.need = "In 2000 an estimated 163 million people worldwide had high myopia, which raises the risk of retinal detachment, myopic macular degeneration, glaucoma and cataract. Ordinary glasses correct blurred distance vision. Myopia-control lenses can slow elongation, but after withdrawal the eye can resume growth typical of untreated myopia. Children who kept distant images in focus as their eyes grew could avoid early myopia and its associated risk of high myopia. Whether childhood treatment prevents later sight loss remains uncertain.". Reason: The current paragraph gives the size of the prevalence study but omits its burden estimate and the clinical difference between retaining a treatment gain and maintaining clear vision as the eye grows.

add statement by National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2024: "both human and animal studies to investigate the mechanisms of emmetropization and myopia". Reason: Recommendation 6-1 names the emmetropization mechanism more specifically than the existing statements on myopia treatment.

edit m1: criterion = "In developing animal eyes, positive lenses focus images in front of the retina and slow axial elongation. Negative lenses focus images behind the retina and accelerate axial elongation. For each sign, the resulting refractive shift must reduce the error imposed by the lens. Lens power and exposure duration depend on the species."; set_by = "Experimental emmetropization community, as described in sections 3.4 and 8 of the 2019 IMI experimental-models report"; threshold_quote = "Imposing hyperopic or myopic defocus in animal models results in compensatory changes in eye growth that reduces the imposed refractive error."; threshold_ref = 4; refs = [4, 9, 13]. Reason: The criterion mixes the lens-compensation test with its publication history, and the quoted convention appears in the IMI report’s summary points.

edit m2: title = "Human eyes shorten with +3 D defocus and lengthen with \u22123 D defocus after 60 minutes."; criterion = "Measure optical axial length from the anterior cornea to the retinal pigment epithelium at baseline and after 60 minutes of monocular defocus. Test +3 D and \u22123 D on separate days, with the fellow eye optimally corrected and a separate no-defocus control condition. Mean optical axial length must decrease from baseline with +3 D and increase with \u22123 D. This assay measures an acute biometric response."; threshold_quote = "Significant changes in optical axial length occurred in human subjects after 60 minutes of monocular defocus."; threshold_ref = 10. Reason: The published changes in micrometres are observations from one sample, whereas the assay tests the direction of the short-term change from baseline.

add milestone after m2: "Fewer initially nonmyopic children develop myopia over two years with treatment than with placebo.". Reason: The existing pediatric efficacy milestone starts after myopia develops and cannot establish whether an intervention delays onset in the population named in the completion test.

edit m3: criterion = "Randomize children who already have myopia to treatment or a concurrent control. Compare change from baseline to three years in both primary outcomes. The treatment group must show less axial elongation and a smaller shift toward myopia in cycloplegic spherical-equivalent refraction."; threshold_quote = "Primary outcome measures were the change in cycloplegic spherical equivalent refraction and axial length."; threshold_ref = 11; refs = [11, 7]. Reason: The three-year randomized comparison has two primary outcomes, while the sample counts, observed effects and modeled emmetropic cohort are evidence about the test.

edit m4: title = "FDA authorizes a device for slowing myopia progression in children."; criterion = "FDA authorizes marketing of the device with an indication explicitly covering slower myopia progression in children. Apply the age at treatment initiation, refractive range and other eligibility conditions in that device\u2019s authorized labeling. An indication limited to optical correction is insufficient."; set_by = "US Food and Drug Administration, pediatric indications for use in PMA P180035 and De Novo classification DEN250016"; threshold_quote = "for slowing the progression of myopia in children"; threshold_ref = 16; refs = [8, 16]. Reason: FDA has authorized a pediatric progression indication through both premarket approval and De Novo classification, and each device has its own labeled population.

edit m5: criterion = "Follow children for at least one year after stopping treatment. Compare axial elongation and progression of cycloplegic spherical-equivalent refraction with rates expected in age-matched untreated myopic eyes over the same interval. Both comparisons must support retention of the accrued gain without excess progression. Report uncertainty in each difference so readers can judge how much rebound is compatible with the data."; threshold_quote = "Studies designed to evaluate potential rebound should have a minimum 1 year follow-up after stopping treatment"; threshold_ref = 7. Reason: The withdrawal criterion needs the age-matched untreated comparator and uncertainty in the comparison, while the MiSight estimates belong with the result.
structure = parallel. Reason: Onset and progression trials have different entry populations, and FDA authorized Stellest on a 24-month analysis without waiting for the three-year efficacy milestone.
remove not found 2. Reason: The full 1988 paper gives the group sizes, including ten chicks fitted binocularly with the same lens power and eight fitted with opposite signs.

add not found: "No National Academies or IMI statement disputing the feasibility or value of restoring durable emmetropization was located.". Reason: The available statements address mechanisms and treatments but leave institutional disagreement about durable restoration unresolved.
